tldr: In robot-to-human object handovers, combining temporal tactile encoding (TTE) covering about 1 second with compliance control that yields to external forces successfully distinguishes accidental contact from genuine taking intent, achieving smooth and safe handovers.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed system. Head RGB camera images, 3-axis forces estimated from fingertip tactile sensors (Xela), and joint states are integrated into a VLA model (GR00T) equipped with a temporal tactile encoder (TTE), which outputs target end-effector positions. In addition, low-level compliance control allows the hands to yield flexibly to the person's pulling force.
overview:
The task of a robot handing an object to a person is crucial in caregiving and collaborative work, but deciding exactly when to release the object is harder than it seems. Letting go too early causes the object to drop, while letting go too late forces the human into a tug-of-war with the robot, leading to discomfort and danger. Camera images alone cannot tell whether a person genuinely intends to pull the object, just bumped into it accidentally, or pushed it in the wrong direction.

To tackle this, the authors treated bimanual object handover using the humanoid robot "ergoCub" as an intrinsically multimodal problem. They designed a Temporal Tactile Encoder (TTE) that compresses past fingertip tactile signals spanning about 0.9 seconds into a low-dimensional representation, and finetuned the vision-language-action (VLA) foundation model "NVIDIA Isaac GR00T 1.5". Furthermore, they incorporated a low-level compliance controller so the robot naturally yields to human pulling forces rather than resisting them.

Evaluation was conducted in two stages. First, open-loop evaluations confirmed that temporal encoding drastically reduces false releases compared to instantaneous tactile inputs. Next, real-robot handover experiments with 10 human subjects (300 trials in total) were carried out to ablate tactile history and compliance control.

As a result, the proposed approach achieved a 93% overall success rate, significantly outperforming the baselines across timely success within a prescribed time limit (92%), response delay (median 1.70 s), and required pulling force (4.07 N). Tactile history provides reliable release decisions while compliance control enables smooth and comfortable physical interaction, demonstrating a remarkable complementary synergy between the two.
contributions: Built a multimodal imitation learning framework for humanoid bimanual handover that integrates RGB images, fingertip tactile sensing, temporal tactile encoding, and compliance control.

Proposed an autoencoder-based Temporal Tactile Encoder (TTE) that compresses contact history and force direction changes over ~0.9 seconds to prevent false releases caused by transient tactile spikes.

Conducted ablation experiments isolating the respective roles of tactile history and compliance control, demonstrating their synergistic effect in improving intent estimation accuracy and user comfort.

Demonstrated significant improvements in objective success rate, responsiveness, and pulling force reduction, as well as subjective safety and smoothness, through 300 real-robot trials across 10 participants and questionnaires.

sections.heading: Why does a robot struggle with when to let go?
sections.summary: In handover tasks, releasing too early causes dropped objects while releasing too late leads to an uncomfortable tug-of-war, making precise release timing critical. Because vision alone cannot tell accidental contact apart from genuine taking intent, this work proposes combining temporal tactile history with flexible compliance control.
sections.details:
For assistive and service robots working alongside humans, object handover is an essential primitive behavior. However, mistimed releases create serious issues. If the robot lets go too early, the dropped object can cause damage or injury; if it lets go too late, the receiver must pull forcefully against the robot, inducing discomfort and hazards. Inferring taking intent is challenging because human motion, contact establishment, grasp formation, pulling forces, and load transfer are all entangled in complex ways. With camera images alone, contact surfaces are often occluded and fine-grained force interactions remain invisible, making it difficult to distinguish an intentional taking action from an accidental touch or transient brush.

Tactile sensors provide a direct window into contact forces, slippage, and local dynamics, but prior work has mostly relied on rule-based release logic or focused on robot-robot or robot-environment contact tasks. How to integrate tactile information into learned policies for human handovers has remained an open question.

Moreover, compliance—the robot's ability to yield softly when a person pulls the object—is also vital. While compliance reduces physical resistance and enhances safety, it introduces a dilemma: the robot's own passive yielding motion can easily be mistaken by the policy as a sign that it should release. Here, tactile feedback serves as the key differentiator between the robot's own compliant deformation and sustained human taking intent.

In this study, based on NVIDIA's VLA foundation model "GR00T 1.5", the authors propose a hierarchical multimodal imitation learning approach combining RGB images, ~1-second temporal tactile features (TTE), proprioception (joint states), and low-level compliance control.

sections.heading: How does this differ from prior work? Moving from rules and manipulation to human collaboration
sections.summary: Most bimanual manipulation and visuo-tactile learning research has targeted autonomous object manipulation, while handovers to humans have largely relied on hand-crafted rules or end-effector trajectory generation. This work sets itself apart by building on a VLA model and having the policy directly learn when to release from dense fingertip tactile history.
sections.details:
Related work in this domain broadly falls into four categories:

- **Model-based bimanual manipulation**: Methods optimizing grasp forces for multi-fingered hands, along with impedance and admittance control, have been developed to guarantee stability and safety. However, they rely on explicit control laws and do not directly learn release behaviors from multimodal human interactions.
- **Visuo-tactile learning**: Recent frameworks such as TactileAloha and Bi-Touch have advanced tactile-driven learning for contact-rich bimanual assembly. Yet, these primarily address tasks where a robot manipulates static objects or environments, unlike human handovers where the robot must infer whether the partner has securely taken the object.
- **Human-robot handover**: Many studies have investigated handover trajectory generation and intent prediction, including dynamic handovers paired with impedance control. However, most efforts focus on where and how to move the hands, leaving the crucial release decision to manual force thresholds or simple visual cues.
- **Release decisions via contact sensing**: Adaptive release using wrist force-torque sensors or tactile gloves has been proposed, but dedicated control heuristics and rule-based thresholds remain dominant. Furthermore, recent VLA foundation models for humanoids (such as NVIDIA Isaac GR00T) have not yet incorporated high-frequency fingertip tactile streams for physical human interaction.

This work is novel in that it moves away from predefined release rules, enabling a VLA model to learn release decisions directly from vision, tactile history, and proprioception via imitation learning.

sections.heading: Temporal tactile encoding and hierarchical compliance control
sections.summary: Demonstration data was gathered via Meta Quest 3 teleoperation on the humanoid robot ergoCub. An autoencoder compresses high-frequency tactile data spanning ~0.9 seconds into compact features (TTE) for the VLA model GR00T, which coordinates with low-level compliance control.
sections.details:
### III-A Task and Platform
The humanoid robot "ergoCub" was used for evaluation. The task begins with the robot holding a box with both hands; once the receiver firmly grasps and pulls the object, the robot opens its hands to release it. The robot is equipped with a head RGB camera and 3-axis tactile sensors on its fingertips.

### III-B Teleoperation and Data Collection
A teleoperation system was built using a Meta Quest 3. The operator's hand poses and headset orientation were tracked and mapped to Cartesian reference commands for the robot. Robot states, vision, and control commands were logged at 10 Hz using LeRobot, while raw data from Xela tactile sensors was recorded independently with timestamps at approximately 70 Hz.
A total of 500 demonstrations (25 with compliance and 25 without compliance across 8 participants) were collected. To teach the model to distinguish accidental touches from intentional taking, disturbance patterns were deliberately introduced, such as approaching hands without contact then pulling, initially applying force in the wrong direction then pulling, and intermittent contact before pulling. Operators were instructed to release the box roughly 1 second after the subject signaled that they were pulling, allowing the sensors to capture the shift in pulling loads.

### III-C Force Estimation and Temporal Tactile Encoder (TTE)
Magnetic tactile sensors ("Xela") are mounted on four fingertips per hand (excluding thumbs), with 7 taxels per finger. First, a regression model was trained on data collected from an indenter rig to estimate 3-axis contact forces for each finger.
While the policy operates at 10 Hz, the tactile sensors run at high frequency. Rather than simply feeding instantaneous values (24 dimensions), the authors developed a Temporal Tactile Encoding (TTE) module. It passes the past 64 time steps (~0.9 s, size: $64 \times 2 \times 12$) of force history through a fully connected autoencoder, compressing them into a 24-dimensional latent vector. During training, in addition to the reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}$, direction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dir}}$ (evaluating cosine distance of force direction vectors) and temporal difference direction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\mathrm{dir}}$ were incorporated to accurately capture force orientation and its changes over time.

### III-D Compliance and Upper-Body Control
A compliance mechanism was added to the upper-body controller to passively displace the hands according to external forces. Based on the measured fingertip forces $F_{hi}$, the target hand position $P_h$ is passively modified to $P_{h,c}$ via $K_p (P_h - P_{h,c}) + K_d (\dot{P}_h - \dot{P}_{h,c}) = -\sum F_{hi}$ with $K_p=50$ and $K_d=40$. This allows the robot to yield and follow human pulls rather than resisting, shedding contact forces.

### III-E Policy Architecture
The policy is built upon "NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1.5-3B". Given the prompt "Get the box and pass it to human", RGB images, joint states, and tactile vectors (TTE output), the model outputs Cartesian target trajectories for both hands and the head at 10 Hz in action chunks (16 steps ahead, 1.6 s horizon). Inference is re-triggered after executing the first 8 actions.

captions.F2: Overall system block diagram. Demonstrations are gathered in the teleoperation setup on the left. During autonomous execution on the right, tactile features compressed by TTE and camera images are fed into GR00T, whose hand commands pass through the compliance controller to the upper-body controller.

sections.heading: Real-robot evaluation: Synergies between tactile history and compliant control
sections.summary: After open-loop evaluations showed that TTE drastically suppresses false releases compared to instantaneous values, real-robot handover tests were conducted across 300 trials with 10 participants. The full system (P1: TTE + compliance) achieved a 93% success rate, substantially outperforming the tactile-free (P2) and compliance-free (P3) baselines in safety, responsiveness, and perceived smoothness.
sections.details:
### IV-A Stage 1: Instantaneous Force vs. Temporal Tactile Encoder (TTE)
First, using an offline evaluation dataset of 10 episodes containing disturbances like shaking, tapping, and pushing in the wrong direction, a policy taking instantaneous tactile values (A1) was compared against one using TTE history features (A2).
Measuring false activations where the hands opened past a set threshold revealed that A1 crossed the threshold 51 times, whereas A2 did so only 3 times. Crucially, fatal false releases where hands remained open for more than 1.5 seconds occurred 4 times with A1, but 0 times with A2. This proved TTE's decisive effectiveness in filtering out transient force peaks to capture sustained taking intent.

### IV-B Stage 2: Human-Subject Real-Robot Handover Experiments
Ten subjects who did not participate in data collection were recruited to compare three configurations:
- **P1**: Full system (TTE + compliance control)
- **P2**: Compliance only (no tactile TTE)
- **P3**: TTE only (no compliance control)

Each participant performed 10 trials per policy (5 release-intended "R" trials with normal or light pulls, and 5 hold-intended "H" trials with disturbances like taps, wrong directions, or transient tugs), totaling 300 trials.

### Objective Metric Comparisons
- **Success Rate**: P1 achieved an overall success rate of 93% (compared to 82% for P3 and 56% for P2). For timely success—releasing within 2.8 seconds from the onset of pulling—P1 maintained 92%, whereas P3 dropped to 80% and the tactile-free P2 plummeted to 45%.
- **Response Latency and Pulling Force**: Median release latency was shortest for P1 at 1.70 s (2.00 s for P3, 2.35 s for P2), and the peak pulling force required from the human was also lowest for P1 at 4.07 N (4.74 N for P3, 4.67 N for P2). P1 delivered the fastest handovers with the least physical effort.

### Ablation Insights and Failure Modes
P2 (without tactile sensing) suffered frequent false releases, particularly in trials with simple grasping without pulling (T4: 10% success) and transient tugs (T7: 30% success). This occurred because the policy misinterpreted the robot's own compliant deformation as an intentional human pull.
Conversely, in P3 (without compliance), the hands did not yield to the pull, leading participants to forcibly yank the box out before the robot opened its hands, which caused dropped objects in 4% of trials.
The most difficult condition was T9 (short, strong impulsive tugs), where peak force matches genuine taking, challenging all policies. However, as shown in Figure F4, even when subjected to 3.8 N of peak force comparable to a full pull, P1 resisted brief ~0.2 s tugs and only released when the pull was sustained for ~1.5 seconds.

### Subjective Survey Results
On a 7-point Likert scale, P1 outperformed the baselines by a wide margin in perceived smoothness (6.2) and overall satisfaction (6.2). Furthermore, all 10 participants rated P1 as the safest policy, and 9 out of 10 ranked P1 as their overall top choice.

captions.F4: P1 behavior during a hold-intended trial (T5). Even when the subject applies two brief tugs matching the peak force of a genuine pull (3.8 N), the robot holds onto the box. It only opens its hands when the pull is sustained for approximately 1.5 seconds, proving that release is governed by force persistence rather than instantaneous magnitude.

sections.heading: Separating time scales in human-robot physical interaction
sections.summary: Tactile history and compliance control are not mutually exclusive; they complement each other's weaknesses. Fast, low-latency compliance handles physical gentleness, while the high-level VLA model integrates temporal tactile cues for intent recognition. This hierarchy of time scales provides a foundational design principle for human-collaborative robots.
sections.details:
The experimental findings highlight how Temporal Tactile Encoding (TTE) and compliance control fulfill distinct yet complementary roles. Tactile history bears the responsibility for reliability—preventing false releases and correctly identifying taking intent—while compliance dramatically improves comfort and physical safety by yielding naturally to human movement and preventing drops or excessive resistance. Neither component alone can achieve a safe and pleasant handover.

A compelling insight lies in the difference in operating time scales. Low-level compliance operates at the millisecond scale within the fast control loop, functioning as a physical reflex that immediately relieves contact forces. Meanwhile, the learned policy aggregates ~1 second of tactile evidence through TTE, acting as a deliberate reasoning layer that makes reliable release decisions with a slight, intentional temporal horizon.

This hierarchical coupling of a high-speed reactive reflex layer (low-level compliance) and a temporally aggregated reasoning layer (high-level VLA policy) represents a promising architectural blueprint for deploying foundation models like GR00T in real-world human-interactive robotics.

takeaways: In contact-rich human-robot tasks, relying on instantaneous tactile values leads to frequent false triggers from noise and transient contacts; temporal encoding (TTE) summarizing past ~1 s trends is indispensable.
While compliance control reduces user strain, the robot's passive yielding can easily trick policies into false releases, making paired tactile sensing essential.
Hierarchically separating a millisecond-level reactive compliance layer from a high-level VLA reasoning layer based on temporal features works exceptionally well in physical interaction.

Evaluation protocols should quantitatively assess not only successful handovers (R trials) but also the ability to hold firm under intentional disturbances like taps and wrong-direction forces (H trials).
limitations: Short, impulsive tugs of high force (T9 trials) can still occasionally trigger false releases because their instantaneous magnitude matches genuine taking attempts.
Experiments were conducted using only one specific box, leaving generalization to objects with unfamiliar shapes, weights, and stiffness untested.
The system does not yet feature online adaptation to individual human pulling habits or personalized user preferences.
